t: Working up a painless testicular lump
q: Put the steps in the evaluation and treatment of a painless, firm testicular mass in a young man in the best order.
key: Each step prepares for the next: bedside signs and ultrasound establish a solid intratesticular mass, markers and sperm banking are done before treatment alters them, groin orchiectomy gives the diagnosis without breaching scrotal lymphatics, and staging and marker follow-up come only after the primary tumor is removed.
items: Examine the scrotum and transilluminate the mass
Bedside examination first separates a cystic swelling that glows, such as a hydrocele or spermatocele, from a firm mass that blocks light and must be treated as cancer.
Ultrasound confirms a solid intratesticular lesion and separates it from fluid collections and a varicocele outside the testis, before any surgery is planned.
Draw AFP, hCG and LDH before surgery
Preoperative markers suggest the tumor type, contribute to staging and give the baseline needed to judge how fast they fall after removal.
Surgery, chemotherapy and radiation can all impair fertility, so banking is offered before treatment begins in a young man who may want children.
Perform radical inguinal orchiectomy with high ligation of the cord
Removing the testis and cord through the groin avoids the scrotal lymphatics, which drain to inguinal nodes, and provides the tissue diagnosis.
Stage with CT of the abdomen and chest
After the primary tumor is removed, imaging looks for para-aortic nodes and lung spread, the usual routes of testicular tumor metastasis.
Repeat the markers and follow their fall against their half-lives
Markers that decline more slowly than their half-lives signal residual or metastatic disease, which guides further treatment.
